title: Ten Things: ChatGPT and Generative AI (What In-House Counsel Need to Know)
pub: Ten Things You Need to Know as In-House Counsel (tenthings.blog)
author: Sterling Miller

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Associate training: Automation threatens expertise reproduction
st.an: Miller broadly anticipates transformative legal-AI effects, serious unintended consequences and the need for thoughtful governance. However, the supplied evidence does not address automation of junior work, the verification–experience paradox, or reconstruction of associate apprenticeship, so his position on the cluster’s principal proposition cannot be determined.
qs: It will also be packed with unintended consequences, some good and so bad – really bad.
When you get there, be smart and thoughtful about how you, the department, and the company use these tools.

st.t: Legal workforce: Junior pipelines face the sharpest risk
st.an: Miller broadly anticipates major change in legal practice and urges thoughtful adoption, which is compatible with the cluster’s transformation and adaptation themes. However, he provides no position on lawyer displacement, employment evidence, or the cluster’s central claim that junior training pipelines face the sharpest workforce risk.
qs: On that front, I do believe that it will take a long time for ChatGPT to live up to all the hype when it comes to legal work.
When you get there, be smart and thoughtful about how you, the department, and the company use these tools.

st.t: Reliable delivery: Legal engineering bridges capability and service
st.an: The source offers practical tool-selection and low-cost experimentation advice, with some attention to fitting tools into existing in-house workflows and avoiding unspecified pitfalls. However, it does not substantively address the cluster’s central requirements of multidisciplinary implementation, substantive verification, or task-specific evaluation, and relies mainly on product descriptions and personal forecasts.
qs: My advice is to start with the basics (free or low-cost) and keep your eyes open for tools that better fit the world in-house lawyers live in (and do a better job of avoiding the ChatGPT pitfalls, which I outline below).
Watch for this one – it will be a game-changer for in-house lawyers in my opinion.

st.t: Buyer transformation: Legal departments may capture AI gains
st.an: Miller supports the cluster’s core view that generative AI will transform legal work and that in-house counsel should actively shape its use while applying professional judgment. His contribution is primarily predictive and advisory, however; it does not provide evidence that legal departments have already captured operational gains or materially changed purchasing, pricing or staffing.
qs: As in-house lawyers now is not the time to shy away from generative AI, it’s time to run to the fire.
When you get there, be smart and thoughtful about how you, the department, and the company use these tools.

st.t: Legal assistance: Lower cost complicates protection boundaries
st.an: Miller supports the cluster’s core balance: generative AI can provide useful, inexpensive legal assistance and efficiency gains, but its outputs cannot safely be relied upon without human judgment, verification and professional accountability. His focus is in-house legal work rather than consumer access, UPL reform or distributional effects, so his support is strongest on task-specific utility and safeguards.
qs: While I will not set these out in this post, while I was playing with it, I next asked it to “Prepare a simple mutual non-disclosure agreement for a business using Texas law and exclusion jurisdiction in Texas” and got back a usable first draft.

Meaning, if you use generative AI for legal work, you must know what it is doing, you must review the work product, and you must not take anything you get from ChatGPT at face value.[[11]](#_ftn11)  **8.

st.t: Legal copilot: Verification costs define practical value
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s central copilot framing: generative AI can provide rapid, useful first drafts, but lawyers retain professional responsibility and must independently review legal analysis and writing. Its evidence is experiential rather than systematic, so it supports practical utility and verification needs without establishing consistent quality gains.
qs: It won’t replace me (for a long while anyway, if ever) but it clearly can be a very useful tool when used properly.
This is why it is critical that lawyers double-check any material they get from generative AI tools, especially if they are using it for any type of analysis or legal writing.

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: Miller closely supports the cluster’s core proposition: generative AI is more likely to reconfigure and augment legal work than replace lawyers wholesale, while safe adoption requires continued human involvement, comprehensive verification, caution and governance. His account is largely predictive and practical rather than evidence-rich, and it does not materially address apprenticeship risks or workflow-level evaluation.
qs: ChatGPT/generative AI will be another tool you can use to streamline tasks and reduce the amount of mundane work you must deal with (for example [a chatbot to answer frequently asked questions](https://craftycounsel.co.uk/real-life-stories-of-generative-ai-for-in-house-legal-with-andy-cooke/)) and, instead, free you to work on complex, high-value projects where you truly show your value.

Verify everything, trust nothing.[[18]](#_ftn18)  - Develop legal department and company policies regarding the use of ChatGPT (and note the down sides of [all-out bans](https://www.law.com/corpcounsel/2023/05/11/corporate-bans-of-ai-tools-come-with-their-own-risks/?

st.t: Selective delegation: Rapid drafting proves little reliability
st.an: Miller aligns closely with the cluster’s selective-delegation framing: he reports rapid, usable first drafts but treats AI as an assistive tool requiring lawyer review, correction and accountability. His broader efficiency claims are forecasts based on informal experimentation, not systematic evidence of reliability or net productivity.
qs: Same result, a usable first draft produced in a few seconds.

Meaning, if you use generative AI for legal work, you must know what it is doing, you must review the work product, and you must not take anything you get from ChatGPT at face value.[[11]](#_ftn11)  **8.

st.t: Supervised AI: Verification may consume efficiency gains
st.an: The source endorses the cluster’s core supervised-aid model: generative AI can produce useful drafts quickly, but lawyers must remain involved, verify legal work rather than trust outputs at face value, and adopt cautious departmental governance. It reinforces the verification burden but does not directly establish how much of the efficiency gain that burden consumes.
qs: It won’t replace me (for a long while anyway, if ever) but it clearly can be a very useful tool when used properly.

Meaning, if you use generative AI for legal work, you must know what it is doing, you must review the work product, and you must not take anything you get from ChatGPT at face value.[[11]](#_ftn11)  **8.

st.t: Task substitution: Complementarity can still reshape staffing
st.an: Miller supports the core augmentation proposition: generative AI may substantially change legal work while lawyers remain necessary for verification, professional judgment and client-facing responsibility. He does not materially extend the cluster’s analysis of staffing, demand or business-model effects, and his position rests on prediction and professional experience rather than measured employment evidence.
qs: Second, you must validate everything it spits out, another reason why the bar won’t allow AI to replace lawyers (see below for more on the problems with ChatGPT and ethical obligations).

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: Miller accepts the cluster’s core proposition: generative AI can improve bounded legal tasks and materially change work, but it is not a substitute for lawyers. He makes human verification, professional responsibility, low-risk task selection and organisational policies central to safe adoption. His support rests mainly on personal experiments, a reported hallucination incident and predictions rather than systematic evidence, and he does not substantially develop the cluster’s broader operating-model or jagged-frontier analysis.

kp.k: AI should augment rather than replace in-house lawyers
kp.d: Writing in May 2023, Miller predicts substantial job change but considers lawyer replacement highly unlikely. His reasons include continued human involvement required by professional regulation, verification, contextual judgment, critical thinking and clients’ preference for personal advice. These are practitioner arguments and expectations, not measured employment findings; he acknowledges that replacement cannot be ruled out entirely.
qs: It may change it – a lot.
In fact, it needs humans to stay involved, especially when used for legal work.
Still, nothing is 100% guaranteed, so don’t rest on your laurels here, it’s also good to be a little afraid that you might be replaced – even with a machine.

kp.k: Efficiency could expand capacity without changing headcount
kp.d: Miller anticipates that generative AI will streamline mundane work, including frequently asked questions, allowing legal departments to concentrate on complex, high-value projects without large investments or staffing changes. This is a conditional forecast rather than documented department-wide productivity evidence.
qs: allow legal departments to increase efficiency without adding headcount (or cutting headcount) and without having to invest large sums of money.
free you to work on complex, high-value projects where you truly show your value.

kp.k: Prompting becomes a legal skill and potential specialism
kp.d: Miller predicts new roles for lawyers preparing prompts and training systems for particular departments. He recommends that young in-house lawyers position themselves as departmental experts, while stressing that effective prompting takes practice and time. His young-associate analogy presents AI output as work requiring briefing, iteration and correction rather than autonomous reliance.
qs: Generative AI will also create new jobs, including the need for lawyers who specialize in preparing prompts and training the system for the needs of a particular legal department at a particular company.
In short, treat it like a young associate.
If I were a young in-house lawyer today, I would be learning about ChatGPT and positioning myself to be the department expert.

kp.k: Potential applications span legal and administrative workflows
kp.d: Miller lists current applications across ChatGPT and other AI tools: research, drafting, discovery review, litigation prediction, due diligence, contract analysis and redlining, invoice review, meeting transcription, translation, presentations and internal chatbots. The list is an application survey supported by linked sources, not a comparative evaluation; he explicitly cannot vouch for most products.
qs: Lastly, I’ll note that I cannot yet vouch for most of these, but the sources I have used are very reliable:
Negotiate edits to contracts/align contracts to playbooks
Review legal and vendor invoices

kp.k: Personal experiments suggest rapid first-draft production
kp.d: Miller reports that ChatGPT produced an attorney-client privilege explanatory email in seconds, compared with his estimated 10 or 15 minutes to prepare it himself. He also reports usable first drafts of a Texas-law mutual nondisclosure agreement and a mutual indemnity clause. These are personal demonstrations and judgments, not controlled quality or productivity findings; he envisages editing and customization and notes that the general email topic avoided confidential inputs.
qs: saving me the 10 or 15 minutes it would probably take me to put it together
Same result, a usable first draft produced in a few seconds.
It won’t replace me (for a long while anyway, if ever) but it clearly can be a very useful tool when used properly.

kp.k: Human verification is essential to responsible legal use
kp.d: Miller warns that plausible answers, cases and citations may be fabricated, leaving lawyers accountable for checking outputs. Footnote 18 reports a lawyer filing a brief containing fabricated authorities without reviewing them and expresses Miller’s view that failing to check such citations constitutes malpractice. The incident illustrates reliance risk, not a measured hallucination rate or a reported final disciplinary determination.
qs: This is why it is critical that lawyers double-check any material they get from generative AI tools, especially if they are using it for any type of analysis or legal writing.
Verify everything, trust nothing.
Apparently ChatGPT made up cases and citations.
Even assuming the lawyer was that clueless, failing to check citations in a brief generated by ChatGPT is the definition of malpractice in my mind.

kp.k: Professional obligations remain with lawyers and supervisors
kp.d: Miller identifies ABA Model Rules 1.1, 1.4, 1.6, 5.1 and 5.3 as relevant to technological competence, client communication, confidentiality and supervision of lawyers and nonlawyer assistance. He interprets these as requiring informed, supervised AI use and review, and cautions that in-house counsel can face malpractice claims. His footnote expressly distinguishes the Model Rules used for exposition from the rules applicable where a lawyer practices.
qs: Second, under the rules of professional responsibility, you will have many ethical obligations to watch out for and comply with when using generative AI.
Meaning, if you use generative AI for legal work, you must know what it is doing, you must review the work product, and you must not take anything you get from ChatGPT at face value.
but you should always focus on the rules applicable to where you actually practice.

kp.d: Miller warns that prompt inputs may escape confidentiality protections and cites the Samsung employee incident as an example. He recommends fake names and broad inquiries, raises questions about complying with CCPA and GDPR rights, and regards confidentiality fixes as a prerequisite for enterprise use. These are his May 2023 risk assessments and expectations, not findings that every tool has identical data practices.
qs: whatever information you enter into ChatGPT can find its way into the public domain.
And until this is fixed, the tool will not be used at an enterprise level.
How do individuals exercise their right to delete/be forgotten, correct or amend, and get copies?

kp.k: Information and memory limits restrict complex legal analysis
kp.d: As a contemporaneous product snapshot, Miller describes ChatGPT as limited to information through September 2021 and not searching the internet. He gives approximate input limits of 3,000 words for ChatGPT-3.5 and 12,300 words for ChatGPT-4, arguing that these constrain briefs and motions analysis. He also warns about unreliable training material. These are reported limitations at publication, not timeless specifications or benchmark findings.
qs: currently, ChatGPT only uses information made available to it through September 2021 and it does not connect to the internet when searching.
currently, ChatGPT-3.5 can accept about 3,000 words max.
ChatGPT-4 can accept about 12,300 words max.

kp.k: IP, harmful content and cyber risks require scrutiny
kp.d: Miller identifies copyright and trademark infringement, missing or fabricated attribution, offensive outputs, defamation and malicious cybersecurity uses as additional risks. He frames the legality of ingesting protected material under US fair use as unresolved and asks what adverse resolution could mean for tool availability and cost, rather than claiming an established legal outcome.
qs: If not, what does that mean for the future of these tools (and the cost)?
Unless you are using the tool in a closed loop of information, IP infringement is a real risk.
Watch out for this along with defamation issues if you are going to use ChatGPT material in something you will make available to others.

kp.k: Adoption should be staged, collaborative and vendor-aware
kp.d: Miller recommends starting with free products and low-risk tasks, progressing to the paid ChatGPT version and then established suppliers, while monitoring emerging tools tailored to in-house work. He expects integration into Microsoft Office and Word to be particularly consequential because those applications are already embedded in legal workflows. He advocates team experimentation, an internal expert and continuous learning rather than immediate unrestricted deployment.
qs: Start small and with free products and low-risk tasks (understanding the risks) and get your feet wet.
Consider appointing someone (or asking for a volunteer) to become the ChatGPT guru on the legal team.
Watch for this one – it will be a game-changer for in-house lawyers in my opinion.

kp.k: Legal departments should lead governance and internal self-help
kp.d: Miller urges legal teams to develop company and departmental usage policies, consider the downsides of blanket bans, monitor regulation and participate in company-wide adoption decisions. He supports regulation while cautioning against suppressing useful innovation. He also recommends internal FAQ chatbots and document assembly as business self-help services and opportunities to demonstrate the department’s value; this concerns enterprise service delivery, not public access to justice.
qs: I believe regulation is needed, but my hope is that such regulation doesn’t go so far as to kill a promising tool in the cradle.
Find a way to make the department’s AI tools available to the business as part of a self-help initiative, e.g., FAQ chatbot or document assembly tool on your intranet site.
The legal team should be front and center here and leading from the front.

kp.k: Long-term transformation is predicted despite near-term limitations
kp.d: Miller concludes that generative AI represents a potentially historic change in legal practice, but expects substantial time before it fulfills legal-work hype and anticipates serious unintended consequences. The document is explicitly practical practitioner commentary based on reading and personal use, not a systematic empirical study or legal opinion.
qs: On that front, I do believe that it will take a long time for ChatGPT to live up to all the hype when it comes to legal work.
Yet, I have no doubt it will get there.
“Ten Things” is not legal advice nor legal opinion and represents my views only.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Miller predicts augmentation rather than replacement of lawyers, with greater departmental capacity and new AI-specialist work.
pts.d: Sterling Miller argues that generative AI is highly unlikely to replace lawyers in its early stages, although it may substantially change their work. His reasons include continued human involvement required by professional regulation, human verification of outputs, contextual judgment and critical thinking, and clients' preference for personal advice. He expects legal departments eventually to increase efficiency without adding or cutting headcount or making large investments, redirecting lawyers from mundane tasks toward complex, high-value projects. He also predicts new work for lawyers preparing prompts and training systems for particular departments. These are his forecasts, not demonstrated employment outcomes.

pts.k: Miller claims that AI already supports a wide range of legal tasks and can rapidly produce editable first drafts.
pts.d: His May 2023 task inventory spans research, drafting, e-discovery review, due diligence, contract analysis and redlining, litigation prediction, invoice review, summaries, translation, meeting transcription and business-facing FAQ chatbots. The inventory combines ChatGPT with other named AI products; it does not establish that ChatGPT alone performs all of these functions. In his own trials, Miller describes an explanatory email, a mutual NDA and a mutual indemnity clause as usable starting points generated in seconds. He presents these as supervised drafting assistance, not autonomous legal advice.

pts.k: Miller predicts routine integration into legal departments, while expecting full transformation to take considerably longer.
pts.d: Miller expects generative AI to become a natural extension of daily in-house work. He singles out Microsoft's integration into Office and Word as potentially game-changing because these are tools in-house lawyers already use. His long-term optimism is qualified by the expectation that legal AI will take a long time to fulfil the hype and will produce significant unintended consequences.

pts.k: Miller argues that AI introduces verification duties and corporate risks that preserve a central role for lawyers.
pts.d: He says lawyers must review AI work rather than rely on it directly because systems can fabricate answers and citations and lack accountability. He identifies confidentiality, privacy, intellectual-property, offensive-content and cybersecurity risks, alongside information and context limitations. He presents AI governance, company policies and oversight of adoption as opportunities for in-house lawyers to demonstrate value. His claim that unresolved confidentiality prevents enterprise use is a contemporaneous assertion, not a finding about all products or later adoption.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The principal evidence is Miller's experimentation, professional experience and linked secondary material, rather than systematic measurement.
pts.d: Miller reports reading extensively and trying multiple prompts. His clearest productivity example is an attorney-client privilege email generated in seconds versus his estimate of 10–15 minutes to compose it himself. This is an anecdotal estimate of drafting time, not a controlled study or a measurement of net savings after verification and editing. He reports usable NDA and indemnity drafts but does not reproduce them. Most product capabilities rest on linked sources that he considers reliable, with an explicit caveat that he cannot personally vouch for most. Employment, headcount and long-term transformation claims are supported by professional reasoning and commentary links, without quantified labour-market evidence.

pts.k: Risk and supervision claims draw on professional rules, reported incidents and personal encounters with fabricated citations.
pts.d: Miller cites ABA Model Rules 1.1, 1.4, 1.6, 5.1 and 5.3 for his account of competence, communication, confidentiality and supervision obligations, while directing readers to the rules applicable where they practise. He links to reporting on Samsung employees' disclosure of information and the Avianca-related fabricated-citation incident. He uses the latter to illustrate failure to verify legal work, not to supply a measured hallucination rate or report a sanctions outcome. His claim that unchecked output constitutes malpractice is expressly his own opinion. He also reports personally receiving fabricated source references.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The article distinguishes May 2023 capabilities, a possible later-2023 Office rollout, and unspecified eventual gains.
pts.d: The article is explicitly a snapshot dated 31 May 2023. The task inventory concerns what Miller says tools can do then; some products elsewhere in the article are still in testing or available only through early access or waitlists. His Office integration forecast concerns later in 2023. Broader efficiency and transformation predictions have no fixed completion date. His job-security argument is strongest for the early period, though he also says he does not expect all his work to become automatable within his lifetime and acknowledges that replacement is not impossible. Claims about information cutoffs, internet connectivity and context limits describe his account at publication rather than permanent capabilities.

pts.k: Benefits depend on human review, effective prompting, low-risk experimentation and adequate information protection.
pts.d: Miller qualifies productivity claims by the time needed to learn prompting and the possibility of poor results. He recommends treating the system like a young associate whose work requires instruction and correction. He advocates beginning with free tools and low-risk tasks, protecting confidential and personal information, observing applicable ethical rules and introducing departmental and company policies. His sample email avoids confidentiality concerns because its subject is general. He expects privacy problems to be resolved but gives no timetable.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The primary affected group is corporate in-house legal teams and their internal business clients.
pts.d: Miller expects in-house counsel to spend less time on routine work and more on complex advice, while departments gain capacity without necessarily changing headcount. Young in-house lawyers may benefit from becoming departmental AI and prompting experts. Supervisory lawyers remain responsible for compliant use and verification. Corporate executives are presented as still wanting human legal advisers for consequential decisions. Business employees may receive FAQ and document-assembly self-service tools, while companies require legal guidance on adoption, confidentiality, privacy and regulation. These are enterprise legal-service and governance claims, not claims about access to justice or changes in law-firm staffing structures.
